claim: Heme is required for survival of all cells.
source: Heme is required for survival of all cells, and in most eukaryotes, is produced through a series of eight enzymatic reactions.
evidence: This is a statement of established biological knowledge about heme's essential role in cellular survival.

claim: In most eukaryotes, heme is produced through a series of eight enzymatic reactions.
source: Heme is required for survival of all cells, and in most eukaryotes, is produced through a series of eight enzymatic reactions.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the heme biosynthesis pathway.

claim: Erythropoietin (EPO) signaling, together with the GATA1 transcriptional target AKAP10, regulates heme biosynthesis during erythropoiesis at the outer mitochondrial membrane.
source: Here, using zebrafish, murine, and human models, we show that erythropoietin (EPO) signaling, together with the GATA1 transcriptional target, AKAP10, regulates heme biosynthesis during erythropoiesis at the outer mitochondrial membrane.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from multiple model systems (zebrafish, murine, and human) as described in the manuscript.

claim: Ferrochelatase (FECH) is directly phosphorylated by protein kinase A (PKA).
source: This integrated pathway culminates with the direct phosphorylation of the crucial heme biosynthetic enzyme, ferrochelatase (FECH) by protein kinase A (PKA).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro kinase assays and immunoprecipitation experiments shown in the manuscript.

claim: Biochemical, pharmacological, and genetic inhibition of the EPO/AKAP10/PKA signaling pathway results in a block in hemoglobin production.
source: Biochemical, pharmacological, and genetic inhibition of this signaling pathway result in a block in hemoglobin production and concomitant intracellular accumulation of protoporphyrin intermediates.
evidence: This is supported by multiple experimental approaches including pharmacological treatments, AKAP10 knockout, and FECH mutation studies.

claim: Inhibition of the EPO/AKAP10/PKA signaling pathway results in concomitant intracellular accumulation of protoporphyrin intermediates.
source: Biochemical, pharmacological, and genetic inhibition of this signaling pathway result in a block in hemoglobin production and concomitant intracellular accumulation of protoporphyrin intermediates.
evidence: This is supported by HPLC analysis showing increased PPIX in FECH mutant cells.

claim: Aberrant PKA signaling is implicated in the pathogenesis of hematologic diseases.
source: Broadly, our results implicate aberrant PKA signaling in the pathogenesis of hematologic diseases.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental findings showing PKA's role in heme biosynthesis and erythropoiesis.

claim: The erythroid transcriptional program works in concert with post-translational mechanisms to regulate heme metabolism during normal development.
source: We propose a unifying model in which the erythroid transcriptional program works in concert with post-translational mechanisms to regulate heme metabolism during normal development.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the integration of findings about GATA1-mediated AKAP10 expression and PKA-mediated FECH phosphorylation.

claim: Heme biosynthesis involves eight enzymatic reactions that occur both in the cytosol and mitochondria.
source: Heme biosynthesis is a fundamental biological process that is highly conserved and involves eight enzymatic reactions that occur both in the cytosol and mitochondria (Severance and Hamza, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: In vertebrates, the most recognized role of heme is to serve as the oxygen-binding moiety in hemoglobin expressed by red blood cells (RBCs).
source: In vertebrates, the most recognized role of heme is to serve as the oxygen-binding moiety in hemoglobin expressed by red blood cells (RBCs).
evidence: This is established knowledge about heme's function in vertebrates.

claim: During RBC maturation, heme metabolism genes are robustly upregulated.
source: During RBC maturation, heme metabolism genes are robustly upregulated (Chung et al., 2012; Nilsson et al., 2009; Yien et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Mutations in heme metabolism genes are most commonly associated with hematologic defects in humans.
source: Not surprisingly, mutations in these genes are most commonly associated with hematologic defects in humans, underscoring the importance for a better understanding of the factors regulating heme biosynthesis.
evidence: This is established knowledge from clinical genetics.

claim: Loss-of-function mutations in FECH are strongly associated with erythropoietic protoporphyria (EPP).
source: In particular, loss-of-function mutations in FECH (EC 4.99.1.1), which encodes the terminal rate-limiting enzyme in heme production, is strongly associated with the disease erythropoietic protoporphyria (EPP) (Balwani and Desnick, 2012; Langendonk et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical literature.

claim: FECH encodes the terminal rate-limiting enzyme in heme production.
source: In particular, loss-of-function mutations in FECH (EC 4.99.1.1), which encodes the terminal rate-limiting enzyme in heme production, is strongly associated with the disease erythropoietic protoporphyria (EPP) (Balwani and Desnick, 2012; Langendonk et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge about FECH's role in heme biosynthesis.

claim: Previous genetic analyses using RBCs have identified several mechanisms regulating heme metabolism, most of which are transcriptional networks controlling mRNA expression of heme metabolism genes.
source: Previous genetic analyses using RBCs have identified several mechanisms regulating heme metabolism most of which are transcriptional networks controlling mRNA expression of heme metabolism genes (Amigo et al., 2011; Handschin et al., 2005; Kardon et al., 2015; Nilsson et al., 2009; Phillips and Kushner, 2005; Shah et al., 2012; Shaw et al., 2006; Wingert et al., 2005; Yien et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Transcription-independent signaling mechanisms regulating heme production are poorly understood.
source: Currently, however, transcription-independent signaling mechanisms regulating heme production are poorly understood (Chen et al., 2009; Paradkar et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations indicating limited prior knowledge in this area.

claim: During red blood cell (RBC) development, PKA expression becomes increased at the mitochondrial outer membrane through AKAP10-dependent recruitment.
source: During red blood cell (RBC) development, PKA expression becomes increased at the mitochondrial outer membrane (OM) through AKAP10-dependent recruitment.
evidence: This is supported by proteomics data, immunoblotting, and AKAP10 knockout experiments.

claim: Mitochondrial outer membrane PKA catalytic (PKAc) subunits become disengaged from the autoinhibitory PKA regulatory (PKAr) subunits through direct interaction with phosphorylated STAT5 downstream of EPOR activation.
source: We found that OM PKA catalytic (PKAc) subunits become disengaged from the autoinhibitory PKA regulatory (PKAr) subunits through direct interaction with phosphorylated STAT5 downstream of EPOR activation.
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation experiments showing STAT5-PKAc complex formation.

claim: FECH phosphorylation by PKA triggers upregulation of its activity that is required to support erythropoiesis in vivo.
source: Furthermore, we demonstrate that FECH is a kinase target of OM PKA and its phosphorylation triggers upregulation of its activity that is required to support erythropoiesis in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro enzyme activity assays, kinetic analyses, and in vivo zebrafish and mouse experiments.

claim: Erythroid differentiation is associated with elevated mitochondrial expression of FECH, ATPIF1, and ABCB10.
source: As expected, erythroid differentiation was associated with the elevated mitochondrial expression of a number of mitochondrial proteins known to have a role in erythropoiesis such as FECH, ATPIF1, and ABCB10 while the expression of housekeeping proteins such as components of the mitochondrial transport and protein translation machinery were relatively unchanged (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The expression of housekeeping proteins such as components of the mitochondrial transport and protein translation machinery were relatively unchanged during erythroid differentiation.
source: As expected, erythroid differentiation was associated with the elevated mitochondrial expression of a number of mitochondrial proteins known to have a role in erythropoiesis such as FECH, ATPIF1, and ABCB10 while the expression of housekeeping proteins such as components of the mitochondrial transport and protein translation machinery were relatively unchanged (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Increased expression of PKA regulatory (PKAr; PRKAR1A, PRKAR2A, PRKAR2B) and catalytic (PKAc; PRKACA and PRKACB) subunits was found in mitochondria-enriched fractions during erythroid differentiation.
source: Strikingly, we also found increased expression of PKA regulatory (PKAr; PRKAR1A, PRKAR2A, PRKAR2B) and catalytic (PKAc; PRKACA and PRKACB) subunits in mitochondria-enriched fractions (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Increased total expression of PKA subunits occurs in maturing erythroid cells.
source: We independently confirmed these results using immunoblotting with isoform-specific antibodies where we also found increased total expression of these PKA subunits in maturing erythroid cells (Figure 1D and E).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figures 1D and E.

claim: PRKACG is only present in humans and not found in murine models.
source: We failed to detect PRKACG because it is only present in humans and not found in our murine model (Kirschner et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work on PKA isoform distribution.

claim: PRKAR1B expression is restricted to neurons.
source: In addition, we also could not detect PRKAR1B since its expression is restricted to neurons (Kirschner et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work on PKA isoform distribution.

claim: The majority of PKA subunits are sensitive to proteinase K activity, similar to TOM20.
source: Immunoblot analysis of untreated and treated mitochondria revealed that the majority of PKA subunits were sensitive to proteinase K activity similar to TOM20 while VDAC1, a mitochondrial outer membrane (OM) marker known to be resistant to proteinase K digestion, remained largely unaffected (Figure 2A) (Rapaport, 2003; Shirihai et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by proteinase K digestion assays shown in Figure 2A.

claim: VDAC1, a mitochondrial outer membrane (OM) marker, is resistant to proteinase K digestion.
source: Immunoblot analysis of untreated and treated mitochondria revealed that the majority of PKA subunits were sensitive to proteinase K activity similar to TOM20 while VDAC1, a mitochondrial outer membrane (OM) marker known to be resistant to proteinase K digestion, remained largely unaffected (Figure 2A) (Rapaport, 2003; Shirihai et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by proteinase K digestion assays shown in Figure 2A and citations to previous work.

claim: PKA subunits are predominantly present in the outer membrane (OM) fraction of maturing erythroid cells.
source: Biochemical fractionation of the mitochondria OM, intermembrane space (IMS), and mitoplast (MP) followed by immunoblotting confirmed the predominant presence of PKA subunits in the OM fraction of maturing erythroid cells (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by submitochondrial fractionation experiments shown in Figure 2B.

claim: There is a pronounced increase in the mitochondrial expression of AKAP10 during erythroid differentiation.
source: Interestingly, although we failed to detect PAP7 and AKAP1 in our proteomics analysis, we found a pronounced increase in the mitochondrial expression of AKAP10 (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: This is supported by proteomics data and immunoblotting shown in Figures 2C and D.

claim: Mitochondrial AKAP10 in maturing erythrocytes is sensitive to proteinase K digestion.
source: Similar to our earlier data with PKA subunits, mitochondrial AKAP10 in maturing erythrocytes is sensitive to proteinase K digestion and primarily found in the OM fraction in maturing erythroid cells (Figure 2E and F).
evidence: This is supported by proteinase K digestion assays shown in Figure 2E.

claim: AKAP10 is primarily found in the outer membrane (OM) fraction in maturing erythroid cells.
source: Similar to our earlier data with PKA subunits, mitochondrial AKAP10 in maturing erythrocytes is sensitive to proteinase K digestion and primarily found in the OM fraction in maturing erythroid cells (Figure 2E and F).
evidence: This is supported by submitochondrial fractionation experiments shown in Figure 2F.

claim: AKAP10 expression increases in maturing erythroid cells and is a downstream target of the GATA1 erythroid lineage master transcription factor.
source: High-throughput expression analysis has previously shown that AKAP10 expression increases in maturing erythroid cells and is a downstream target of the GATA1 erythroid lineage master transcription factor (Fujiwara et al., 2009; Zhang et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous high-throughput expression studies.

claim: AKAP10 knockout cells have reduced levels of mitochondrial PKA subunits both in intact preparations and in outer membrane-specific fractions.
source: However, KO cells had reduced the levels of mitochondrial PKA subunits both in intact preparations as well as in OM-specific fractions (Figure 2J and K).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figures 2J and K.

claim: AKAP10 recruits PKA to the outer mitochondrial membrane during red cell development.
source: These results strongly suggest that AKAP10 recruits PKA to the outer mitochondrial membrane during red cell development and connects the GATA1 transcriptional program to the PKA signaling pathway.
evidence: This is inferred from the AKAP10 knockout experiments showing reduced mitochondrial PKA localization.

claim: AKAP10 connects the GATA1 transcriptional program to the PKA signaling pathway.
source: These results strongly suggest that AKAP10 recruits PKA to the outer mitochondrial membrane during red cell development and connects the GATA1 transcriptional program to the PKA signaling pathway.
evidence: This is inferred from the combination of GATA1 regulation of AKAP10 and AKAP10's role in PKA localization.

claim: Compounds that activate PKA such as 8-Br-cAMP and forskolin cause an increase in the proportion of hemoglobinized cells.
source: Compounds that activate PKA such as 8-Br-cAMP and forskolin both caused an increase in the proportion of hemoglobinized cells as shown by o-dianisidine staining, which can be blocked by PKA antagonists H-89 or PKI (14-22) (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by o-dianisidine staining experiments shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The effects of PKA activators on hemoglobinization can be blocked by PKA antagonists H-89 or PKI (14-22).
source: Compounds that activate PKA such as 8-Br-cAMP and forskolin both caused an increase in the proportion of hemoglobinized cells as shown by o-dianisidine staining, which can be blocked by PKA antagonists H-89 or PKI (14-22) (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by o-dianisidine staining experiments shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Treatment with dimethyl-prostaglandin E2 (dmPGE2) increases the proportion of hemoglobinized cells.
source: An increase in the proportion of hemoglobinized cells was also observed when we treated MEL cells with dimethyl-prostaglandin E2 (dmPGE2) (Figure 3B), which is a more stable analog of prostaglandin E2 (PGE2) that has a physiologic role during multiple aspects of hematopoiesis (Goessling et al., 2009; North et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by o-dianisidine staining experiments shown in Figure 3B.

claim: dmPGE2 is a more stable analog of prostaglandin E2 (PGE2) that has a physiologic role during multiple aspects of hematopoiesis.
source: An increase in the proportion of hemoglobinized cells was also observed when we treated MEL cells with dimethyl-prostaglandin E2 (dmPGE2) (Figure 3B), which is a more stable analog of prostaglandin E2 (PGE2) that has a physiologic role during multiple aspects of hematopoiesis (Goessling et al., 2009; North et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work on PGE2 in hematopoiesis.

claim: The effects of dmPGE2 on hemoglobinization can be inhibited by PKI (14-22).
source: The effects of dmPGE2 can be similarly inhibited by PKI (14-22) (Figure 3C), underscoring the specificity of dmPGE2 signaling via PKA.
evidence: This is supported by o-dianisidine staining experiments shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The PKC inhibitor, bis-indolylmaleimide II, cannot block the effects of PKA activation on heme synthesis.
source: In contrast to PKA inhibition, the PKC inhibitor, bis-indolylmaleimide II, could not block the effects of PKA activation suggesting that the observed changes in heme synthesis are specific for PKA (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by o-dianisidine staining experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: AKAP10-knockout maturing erythroid cells exhibit a deficit in hemoglobinization compared to wild-type controls.
source: Compared to wild-type controls, AKAP10-KO maturing erythroid cells exhibited a deficit in hemoglobinization (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by o-dianisidine staining experiments shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Knockdown of AKAP10 expression using shRNAs results in reduced hemoglobinization.
source: This defect was also observed when AKAP10 expression was inhibited using two distinct shRNAs (Figure 3E and F).
evidence: This is supported by shRNA knockdown experiments shown in Figures 3E and F.

claim: akap10 morphants in zebrafish are anemic with decreased hemoglobinization.
source: Remarkably, akap10 morphants were anemic with decreased hemoglobinization (Figure 3H, red arrowheads) compared to control embryos.
evidence: This is supported by zebrafish morpholino experiments shown in Figure 3H.

claim: akap10 morphants have reduced RBC counts.
source: Flow-cytometry analysis revealed that akap10 morphants had reduced RBC counts (Figure 3I).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry analysis shown in Figure 3I.

claim: Mitochondrial outer membrane PKA signaling is required for proper heme production and RBC development in vivo.
source: Together, our data suggest that mitochondrial OM PKA signaling is required for proper heme production and RBC development in vivo.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined results of AKAP10 knockout in cells and akap10 morpholino experiments in zebrafish.

claim: Of the mitochondrial heme enzymes ALAS2, PPOX, CPOX, and FECH, the only enzyme with a predicted high-confidence PKA site is FECH at Thr116.
source: Of the mitochondrial enzymes ALAS2, PPOX, CPOX, and FECH, the only enzyme with a predicted high-confidence PKA site (R/K-R/K-X-S/T-Z, where X is any amino acid and Z is an uncharged residue) is FECH at Thr116 (human FECH and Thr115 for murine FECH) (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is based on computational prediction of PKA phosphorylation motifs.

claim: The PKA phosphorylation site at Thr116 in FECH is evolutionarily conserved.
source: This residue is evolutionarily conserved and is present on one of the lips of the active site pocket positioned in the middle of a long α-helix (Figure 4B–D).
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment shown in Figure 4B and structural analysis.

claim: Thr116 is present on one of the lips of the active site pocket positioned in the middle of a long α-helix.
source: This residue is evolutionarily conserved and is present on one of the lips of the active site pocket positioned in the middle of a long α-helix (Figure 4B–D).
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis shown in Figures 4C and D.

claim: In its unphosphorylated form, the side chain hydroxyl group of Thr116 forms a hydrogen bond with His86.
source: In its unphosphorylated form, the side chain hydroxyl group of Thr116 (colored fuchsia) is sandwiched between His86 (colored blue) and Leu87 on an adjacent α-helix, forming a hydrogen bond with His86 (Figure 4C and D) (Wu et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis shown in Figures 4C and D and a citation to previous structural work.

claim: Phosphorylation of Thr116 would cause movement of the Thr116 α-helix away from the His86 α-helix, shifting the Thr116-containing α-helix closer inwards towards the active site pocket opening and the porphyrin ring.
source: Structural modeling suggests that the bulk of the added phosphate on the side chain of Thr116 would cause movement of the Thr116 α-helix away from the His86 α-helix, and thereby, shift the Thr116-containing α-helix closer inwards towards the active site pocket opening and the porphyrin ring (shown in red) (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: This is based on structural modeling using the FECH crystal structure.

claim: Phosphorylation of Thr116 may destabilize the FECH structure sufficiently to allow for more efficient movement of the active site lip during catalysis.
source: Such a modification may also destabilize the structure sufficiently to allow for more efficient movement of the active site lip during catalysis.
evidence: This is a speculation based on structural modeling.

claim: FECH is directly phosphorylated by PKA in an ATP-dependent fashion.
source: This experiment showed that FECH is directly phosphorylated by PKA in an ATP-dependent fashion (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro kinase assays shown in Figure 4E.

claim: In vitro, 9.8 ± 3.2% of purified FECH was phosphorylated after 30 min.
source: Using [γ-32P]-ATP labeling, we calculated that, in vitro, 9.8 ± 3.2% of purified FECH was phosphorylated after 30 min.
evidence: This is based on radioactive ATP labeling experiments.

claim: Substitution of Thr116 with Ala (T116A) abolished FECH phosphorylation by PKA.
source: Substitution of Thr116 with Ala (T116A) abolished this phosphorylation (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro kinase assays with mutant FECH shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Mutation of either Lys113 (K113L) or Arg114 to Leu (R114L) reduced FECH phosphorylation.
source: In addition, consistent with the preference of PKAc for positively charged residues at the −3 and −2 positions (Smith et al., 2011), mutation of either Lys113 (K113L) or Arg114 to Leu (R114L) similarly reduced FECH phosphorylation (Figure 4F), strongly indicating that Thr116 of human FECH constitutes a bona fide PKA target.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro kinase assays with mutant FECH shown in Figure 4F and a citation about PKA substrate specificity.

claim: Thr116 of human FECH constitutes a bona fide PKA target.
source: In addition, consistent with the preference of PKAc for positively charged residues at the −3 and −2 positions (Smith et al., 2011), mutation of either Lys113 (K113L) or Arg114 to Leu (R114L) similarly reduced FECH phosphorylation (Figure 4F), strongly indicating that Thr116 of human FECH constitutes a bona fide PKA target.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined results of in vitro kinase assays with wild-type and mutant FECH.

claim: Immunoprecipitated FECH from differentiated MEL cells can be detected by two different phospho-threonine antibodies.
source: Immunoprecipitated FECH from differentiated MEL cells was detected by two different phospho-threonine antibodies—one targeting the Lys-X-X-pThr motif and another recognizing the pThr-Pro sequence (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation and immunoblotting experiments shown in Figure 4G.

claim: High-dose forskolin treatment increased phosphorylation of FECH in differentiating MEL cells.
source: High-dose forskolin treatment also increased phosphorylation of FECH in differentiating MEL cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation and immunoblotting experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Inhibition of outer membrane PKA with loss of AKAP10 resulted in diminished FECH Thr115 phosphorylation.
source: Conversely, inhibition of OM PKA with loss of AKAP10 resulted in diminished FECH Thr115 phosphorylation (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation and immunoblotting experiments in AKAP10 knockout cells shown in Figure 4H.

claim: PKA becomes localized at the mitochondria outer membrane of maturing erythroid cells and directly phosphorylates FECH.
source: In toto, our results support a model where PKA becomes localized at the mitochondria OM of maturing erythroid cells and directly phosphorylates FECH.
evidence: This is a model inferred from the combined results of PKA localization, AKAP10 function, and FECH phosphorylation experiments.

claim: FECH is phosphorylated by protein kinase C (PKC).
source: Past work has demonstrated that FECH is phosphorylated by protein kinase C (PKC) (Sakaino et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: PKC-mediated FECH phosphorylation occurs in a domain buried within an inaccessible hydrophobic fold that did not directly impact enzyme catalysis.
source: PKC-mediated FECH phosphorylation occurs in a domain buried within an inaccessible hydrophobic fold that did not directly impact enzyme catalysis (Sakaino et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: PKA-mediated phosphorylation of FECH results in an approximately two-fold increase in ferrochelatase activity in vitro.
source: Significantly more radioactivity can be detected when purified His-tagged human FECH was added alone to the metalation reaction (Figure 5A) and the addition of purified PKAc to the reaction to catalyze the phosphorylation of FECH resulted in an approximately two-fold increase in 55Fe measurements (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro ferrochelatase activity assays shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The increase in FECH activity with PKA phosphorylation is not attributable to PKAc per se, which has no ferrochelatase activity.
source: This increase in activity is not attributable to PKAc per se, which has no ferrochelatase activity, and the reaction is completely DP-substrate dependent (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by control experiments shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Phosphorylation of FECH has a pronounced effect on maximum velocity (vmax) but does not significantly change the Michaelis-Menten (Km) constant.
source: More detailed analysis on enzyme kinetics revealed that phosphorylation had a pronounced effect on maximum velocity (vmax) but did not significantly change the Michaelis-Menten (Km) constant (Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), suggesting that it has no major influence on substrate binding.
evidence: This is supported by kinetic analyses shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Phosphorylation of FECH has no major influence on substrate binding.
source: More detailed analysis on enzyme kinetics revealed that phosphorylation had a pronounced effect on maximum velocity (vmax) but did not significantly change the Michaelis-Menten (Km) constant (Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), suggesting that it has no major influence on substrate binding.
evidence: This is inferred from the kinetic data showing no significant change in Km.

claim: Mitochondria from differentiating MEL cells exposed to high-dose forskolin catalyzed higher deuteroporphyrin metalation compared to mitochondria derived from untreated cells.
source: Mitochondria from differentiating MEL cells exposed to high-dose forskolin catalyzed higher DP metalation compared to mitochondria derived from untreated cells (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by ferrochelatase activity assays using intact mitochondria shown in Figure 5C.

claim: FECH activity is reduced in AKAP10-knockout cells.
source: Conversely, FECH activity was reduced in AKAP10-KO cells that had compromised FECH phosphorylation (Figures 4H and 5D).
evidence: This is supported by ferrochelatase activity assays in AKAP10 knockout cells shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Phosphorylation of FECH at Thr116 by outer membrane PKA increases FECH catalytic activity.
source: These data indicate that phosphorylation of FECH at Thr116 by OM PKA increases FECH catalytic activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined results of in vitro and cellular ferrochelatase activity assays.

claim: EPP patients harboring FECH mutations retain residual FECH activity.
source: EPP patients harboring FECH mutations retain residual FECH activity (Balwani and Desnick, 2012), suggesting that subtle changes in FECH function have important biological implications.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to clinical literature.

claim: Subtle changes in FECH function have important biological implications.
source: EPP patients harboring FECH mutations retain residual FECH activity (Balwani and Desnick, 2012), suggesting that subtle changes in FECH function have important biological implications.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that EPP patients retain residual FECH activity.

claim: FECHT115A mutant protein is similarly induced upon erythroid differentiation compared to wild-type protein.
source: Compared to wild-type protein, FECHT115A mutant protein was similarly induced upon erythroid differentiation and was phosphorylation defective (Figure 5G and H).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: FECHT115A mutant protein is phosphorylation defective.
source: Compared to wild-type protein, FECHT115A mutant protein was similarly induced upon erythroid differentiation and was phosphorylation defective (Figure 5G and H).
evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation and immunoblotting data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: FECHT115A has diminished ferrochelatase activity compared to wild-type.
source: Direct measurements of enzyme activity from intact mitochondria isolated from wild-type and mutant maturing erythroid cells demonstrated that FECHT115A had diminished ferrochelatase activity (Figure 5I).
evidence: This is supported by ferrochelatase activity assays shown in Figure 5I.

claim: Erythroid cells expressing only FECHT115A protein have reduced hemoglobinization.
source: Furthermore, o-dianisidine staining and high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) analysis revealed that erythroid cells expressing only FECHT115A protein had reduced hemoglobinization as well as lower intracellular hemin levels (Figure 5J and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by o-dianisidine staining shown in Figure 5J.

claim: Erythroid cells expressing only FECHT115A protein have lower intracellular hemin levels.
source: Furthermore, o-dianisidine staining and high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) analysis revealed that erythroid cells expressing only FECHT115A protein had reduced hemoglobinization as well as lower intracellular hemin levels (Figure 5J and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by HPLC analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: FECHT115A-expressing cells have elevated accumulation of the upstream, free protoporphyrin IX (PPIX) precursor.
source: Conversely, FECHT115A-expressing cells had concomitantly elevated accumulation of the upstream, free protoporphyrin IX (PPIX) precursor (Figure 5K).
evidence: This is supported by HPLC analysis shown in Figure 5K.

claim: Excess erythroid PPIX accumulation is only found in EPP cases where it serves as a diagnostic marker.
source: Clinically, excess erythroid PPIX accumulation is only found in EPP cases where it serves as a diagnostic marker (Balwani and Desnick, 2012; Whatley et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical literature.

claim: The build-up of PPIX in FECHT115A-expressing cells indicates that this mutation specifically affects FECH function while the upstream heme biosynthetic pathway remains unaffected.
source: The build-up of PPIX in FECHT115A-expressing cells strongly argues that this mutation specifically affects FECH function while the upstream heme biosynthetic pathway remains unaffected.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of PPIX accumulation without changes in upstream pathway components.

claim: During normal and stress erythropoiesis, erythropoietin (EPO) signaling through its cognate receptor tyrosine kinase (EPOR) regulates survival and proliferation of erythroid progenitors.
source: During normal and stress erythropoiesis, erythropoietin (EPO) signaling through its cognate receptor tyrosine kinase (EPOR) regulates survival and proliferation of erythroid progenitors (Kuhrt and Wojchowski, 2015; Testa, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work on EPO signaling.

claim: There is evidence to suggest that EPO/EPOR signaling regulates other key aspects of erythropoiesis beyond survival and proliferation.
source: However, there is evidence to suggest that EPO/EPOR signaling regulates other key aspects of erythropoiesis.
evidence: This is a general statement introducing the rationale for the study.

claim: The study of EPO/EPOR signaling mechanisms has been hampered by the requirement of EPOR signaling in the early stages of the erythropoietic hierarchy.
source: Unfortunately, the study of such mechanisms has been hampered by the requirement of EPOR signaling in the early stages of the erythropoietic hierarchy (Beale and Chen, 1983; Chida et al., 1999; Socolovsky et al., 1999; Testa, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work on EPOR function.

claim: Limiting erythroid iron uptake dramatically ameliorates Polycythemia Vera (PV) symptoms in a murine model expressing constitutively active V617F JAK2.
source: For example, limiting erythroid iron uptake dramatically ameliorates Polycythemia Vera (PV) symptoms in a murine model expressing constitutively active V617F JAK2 (Ishikawa et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work on PV mouse models.

claim: STAT5-mediated transcriptional up-regulation of the transferrin receptor is likely responsible for amelioration of PV symptoms when iron uptake is limited.
source: This is likely due to STAT5-mediated transcriptional up-regulation of the transferrin receptor (Zhu et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work on STAT5 and transferrin receptor regulation.

claim: Neither PV murine models nor EPO overexpressing transgenic mice show any signs of iron overload.
source: Despite this, neither PV murine models nor EPO overexpressing transgenic mice show any signs of iron overload (Li et al., 2011; Vogel et al., 2003), indicating that EPO signaling not only promotes iron uptake in RBCs but also coordinates its physiologic assimilation into heme without excessive iron accumulation.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work on PV and EPO transgenic mouse models.

claim: EPO signaling not only promotes iron uptake in RBCs but also coordinates its physiologic assimilation into heme without excessive iron accumulation.
source: Despite this, neither PV murine models nor EPO overexpressing transgenic mice show any signs of iron overload (Li et al., 2011; Vogel et al., 2003), indicating that EPO signaling not only promotes iron uptake in RBCs but also coordinates its physiologic assimilation into heme without excessive iron accumulation.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that EPO overexpression does not cause iron overload despite increased iron uptake.

claim: EPOR activates several pathways including the janus kinase 2 (JAK2)/signal transducer and activator of transcription 5 (STAT5), mitogen activated protein kinase (MAPK), and phosphatidyl 3'-inositol kinase (PI3K) pathways.
source: EPOR activates several pathways including the janus kinase 2 (JAK2)/signal transducer and activator of transcription 5 (STAT5), mitogen activated protein kinase (MAPK), and phosphatidyl 3'-inositol kinase (PI3K) pathways (Kuhrt and Wojchowski, 2015), leading us to question whether PKA is also activated by EPO.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work on EPOR signaling pathways.

claim: EPOR activation triggers Tyr694 STAT5 phosphorylation.
source: As expected, EPOR activation triggered Tyr694 STAT5 phosphorylation, which was similarly observed with EPO treatment of human UT7 erythroid cells (Figure 6A–C).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figures 6A-C.

claim: EPOR activation triggers CREBSer133 phosphorylation.
source: As expected, EPOR activation triggered Tyr694 STAT5 phosphorylation, which was similarly observed with EPO treatment of human UT7 erythroid cells (Figure 6A–C).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figures 6A-C showing CREB phosphorylation.

claim: CREBSer133 phosphorylation but not STAT5Tyr694 phosphorylation is blocked by PKI (14-22).
source: CREBSer133 phosphorylation but not STAT5Tyr694 phosphorylation was blocked by PKI (14-22) (Figure 6D), indicating that EPOR signaling specifically activates PKA.
evidence: This is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: EPOR signaling specifically activates PKA.
source: CREBSer133 phosphorylation but not STAT5Tyr694 phosphorylation was blocked by PKI (14-22) (Figure 6D), indicating that EPOR signaling specifically activates PKA.
evidence: This is inferred from the selective inhibition of CREB phosphorylation by PKI.

claim: Co-treatment of UT7 cells with the JAK2 inhibitor, Ruxolitinib, robustly inhibited both STAT5Tyr694 and CREBSer133 phosphorylation.
source: In contrast, co-treatment of UT7 cells with the JAK2 inhibitor, Ruxolitinib, robustly inhibited both STAT5Tyr694 and CREBSer133 phosphorylation (Figure 6E), strongly suggesting that PKA lies downstream of the EPOR/JAK2 pathway.
evidence: This is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: PKA lies downstream of the EPOR/JAK2 pathway.
source: In contrast, co-treatment of UT7 cells with the JAK2 inhibitor, Ruxolitinib, robustly inhibited both STAT5Tyr694 and CREBSer133 phosphorylation (Figure 6E), strongly suggesting that PKA lies downstream of the EPOR/JAK2 pathway.
evidence: This is inferred from the inhibition of CREB phosphorylation by JAK2 inhibitor.

claim: Following EPO exposure, PKAc dissociates from PKAr.
source: Co-immunoprecipitation experiments further demonstrated that, following EPO exposure, PKAc dissociated from PKAr (Figure 6F), which is obligate for PKAc kinase activity (Taylor et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Dissociation of PKAc from PKAr is obligate for PKAc kinase activity.
source: Co-immunoprecipitation experiments further demonstrated that, following EPO exposure, PKAc dissociated from PKAr (Figure 6F), which is obligate for PKAc kinase activity (Taylor et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work on PKA regulation.

claim: EPO stimulation results in an increase in FECH phosphorylation.
source: Indeed, EPO stimulation resulted in an increase in FECH phosphorylation (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation and immunoblotting experiments shown in Figure 6G.

claim: Ruxolitinib inhibits phosphorylation of both CREBSer133 and FECHThr116 in human erythroleukemia (HEL) cells that express the constitutively active JAK2V617F mutant protein.
source: Furthermore, Ruxolitinib inhibited phosphorylation of both CREBSer133 and FECHThr116 in human erythroleukemia (HEL) cells that express the constitutively active JAK2V617F mutant protein (Figure 6H and I).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figures 6H and I.

claim: EPO signaling is linked to heme metabolism through PKA.
source: Together, our data link EPO signaling to heme metabolism through PKA.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined results showing EPO activates PKA which phosphorylates FECH.

claim: Early studies failed to detect changes in cAMP levels despite EPO's stimulatory effect on iron incorporation during RBC maturation.
source: This is because early studies failed to detect changes in cAMP levels despite its stimulatory effect on iron incorporation during RBC maturation that is likely mediated by the synergistic effects of CREB on STAT5 transcription (Boer et al., 2002, 2003; Gidari et al., 1971; Schooley and Mahlmann, 1975).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on EPO and cAMP.

claim: EPO's stimulatory effect on iron incorporation during RBC maturation is likely mediated by the synergistic effects of CREB on STAT5 transcription.
source: This is because early studies failed to detect changes in cAMP levels despite its stimulatory effect on iron incorporation during RBC maturation that is likely mediated by the synergistic effects of CREB on STAT5 transcription (Boer et al., 2002, 2003; Gidari et al., 1971; Schooley and Mahlmann, 1975).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Recent evidence indicates that PKAc activation is much more complex involving direct protein-protein interactions with other cell signaling regulators and feedback mechanisms independent of cAMP.
source: However, recent evidence indicates that PKAc activation is much more complex involving direct protein-protein interactions with other cell signaling regulators and feedback mechanisms independent of cAMP (Taylor et al., 2012; Wong and Scott, 2004; Yang et al., 2013, 1995; Zakhary et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work on PKA regulation.

claim: STAT5 forms a complex with PKAc in HEL cells that have constitutive JAK2V617F signaling.
source: Co-immunoprecipitation experiments performed using lysates from HEL cells that have constitutive JAK2V617F signaling revealed that STAT5 formed a complex with PKAc (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The STAT5-PKAc complex formation is sensitive to pharmacologic inhibition of JAK2 function with Ruxolitinib.
source: The STAT5-PKAc complex formation was sensitive to pharmacologic inhibition of JAK2 function with Ruxolitinib (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 7B.

claim: EPO can trigger the formation of the STAT5-PKAc complex.
source: STAT5 only co-precipitated with PKAc in lysates harvested from EPO-stimulated human UT7 erythroid cells (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The fraction of STAT5 that co-precipitates with PKAc is phosphorylated on Tyr694.
source: This fraction of STAT5 was phosphorylated on Tyr694 (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblotting of co-immunoprecipitated proteins shown in Figure 7C.

claim: STAT5 does not co-precipitate with PKAr subunits.
source: In contrast, STAT5 did not co-precipitate with PKAr subunits (Figure 7D), suggesting that phospho-STAT5/PKAc form a distinct complex apart from PKAr.
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Phospho-STAT5/PKAc form a distinct complex apart from PKAr.
source: In contrast, STAT5 did not co-precipitate with PKAr subunits (Figure 7D), suggesting that phospho-STAT5/PKAc form a distinct complex apart from PKAr.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of STAT5-PKAr co-immunoprecipitation.

claim: The phospho-STAT5/PKAc complex can only be found in cell lysates derived from the cytosol but not the mitochondria.
source: Lastly, the phospho-STAT5/PKAc complex can only be found in cell lysates derived from the cytosol but not the mitochondria (Figure 7E) and indicates that at least a fraction of active PKAc can diffuse freely to phosphorylate nuclear CREB (Hagiwara et al., 1993; Mayr and Montminy, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation experiments with fractionated lysates shown in Figure 7E.

claim: At least a fraction of active PKAc can diffuse freely to phosphorylate nuclear CREB.
source: Lastly, the phospho-STAT5/PKAc complex can only be found in cell lysates derived from the cytosol but not the mitochondria (Figure 7E) and indicates that at least a fraction of active PKAc can diffuse freely to phosphorylate nuclear CREB (Hagiwara et al., 1993; Mayr and Montminy, 2001).
evidence: This is inferred from the cytosolic localization of the STAT5-PKAc complex and supported by citations about CREB phosphorylation.

claim: Heme metabolism genes are downstream of GATA1 during RBC development.
source: Heme metabolism genes are downstream of GATA1 during RBC development and regulation of heme production has always been thought to occur at the level of gene transcription (Fujiwara et al., 2009; Handschin et al., 2005; Phillips and Kushner, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work on GATA1 and heme metabolism gene regulation.

claim: Regulation of heme production has always been thought to occur at the level of gene transcription.
source: Heme metabolism genes are downstream of GATA1 during RBC development and regulation of heme production has always been thought to occur at the level of gene transcription (Fujiwara et al., 2009; Handschin et al., 2005; Phillips and Kushner, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work on transcriptional regulation of heme metabolism.

claim: GATA1 is required for very early stages of erythroid development when the demand for heme and hemoglobin is still low.
source: However, GATA1 is required for very early stages of erythroid development when the demand for heme and hemoglobin is still low (Fujiwara et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work on GATA1 function.

claim: Heme metabolism during cell differentiation requires coordinated metabolic alterations dictated by extracellular signaling cues.
source: This raises the possibility that heme metabolism during cell differentiation requires coordinated metabolic alterations dictated by extracellular signaling cues.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observation that GATA1 acts early while heme demand increases later.

claim: EPO is critical for the proliferation and survival of early erythroid progenitors.
source: While it is dispensable for early erythroid specification, EPO is critical for the proliferation and survival of early erythroid progenitors (Kuhrt and Wojchowski, 2015) and promotes their differentiation by increasing iron uptake and reducing 'stemness' potential (Decker, 2016; Ishikawa et al., 2015; Park et al., 2016; Zhu et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work on EPO function.

claim: EPO promotes erythroid differentiation by increasing iron uptake and reducing 'stemness' potential.
source: While it is dispensable for early erythroid specification, EPO is critical for the proliferation and survival of early erythroid progenitors (Kuhrt and Wojchowski, 2015) and promotes their differentiation by increasing iron uptake and reducing 'stemness' potential (Decker, 2016; Ishikawa et al., 2015; Park et al., 2016; Zhu et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work on EPO function.

claim: In the absence of intrinsic apoptotic signals, mitochondrial PKA signaling within the matrix is compartmentalized due to the impermeability of the inner mitochondrial membrane.
source: There is a growing body of evidence that, in the absence of intrinsic apoptotic signals, mitochondrial PKA signaling within the matrix is compartmentalized due to the impermeability of the inner mitochondrial membrane (Acin-Perez et al., 2009; Lefkimmiatis et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work on mitochondrial PKA compartmentalization.

claim: Phosphorylation of matrix proteins can only be achieved by activating signals within the matrix.
source: Under this scenario, phosphorylation of matrix proteins can only be achieved by activating signals within the matrix (Acin-Perez et al., 2009; DiPilato et al., 2004; Lefkimmiatis et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work on mitochondrial PKA signaling.

claim: The import of nuclear-encoded mitochondrial proteins requires the maintenance of these proteins in an unfolded state.
source: The import of nuclear-encoded mitochondrial proteins requires the maintenance of these proteins in an unfolded state (Lodish et al., 2012), which would allow greater accessibility of target motifs.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a textbook on molecular cell biology.

claim: Mitochondrial membrane embedded BAX is first phosphorylated by outer membrane PKA.
source: In support, mitochondrial membrane embedded BAX is, first, phosphorylated by OM PKA (Danial et al., 2003; Harada et al., 1999) and the requirement for protein unfolding during mitochondrial import is consistent with the low level of FECH phosphorylation in vitro (approximately 10%) that we observed.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work on BAX phosphorylation.

claim: Binding of the FECH substrate to the PKA kinase may induce conformational changes that would render the target motif more favorable to modification.
source: It is also very possible that binding of the FECH substrate to the PKA kinase induces conformational changes that would render the target motif more favorable to modification. This mechanism has previously been proposed as a means to prevent 'promiscuous' phosphorylation (Dar et al., 2005; Dey et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a speculation supported by citations to previous work on substrate-induced conformational changes in kinases.

claim: The outer membrane is a prime location for post-translational modifications that would coordinate mitochondrial physiology with overall cellular behavior.
source: Regardless the mechanism, given its exposure to the cytosol and access to proteins destined for mitochondrial localization, the OM is a prime location for such modifications to occur that would coordinate mitochondrial physiology with overall cellular behavior.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the properties of the outer mitochondrial membrane.

claim: Outer membrane PKA is similarly responsive to cytosolic activation mechanisms but remains active much longer and is largely subject to cAMP-independent regulation.
source: Accordingly, studies have shown that OM PKA has unique signaling properties in that it is similarly responsive to cytosolic activation mechanisms but remains active much longer and is largely subject to cAMP-independent regulation (Lefkimmiatis et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work on outer membrane PKA signaling.

claim: Phosphorylated STAT proteins, particularly STAT3 and STAT5, localize to mitochondria.
source: Our work implicates phosphorylated STAT5 as a novel PKAc binding protein that can displace it from autoinhibitory PKAr subunits (Figures 6 and 7) and is corroborated by recent work showing that phospho-STAT proteins, particularly STAT3 and STAT5, localize to mitochondria (Carbognin et al., 2016; Gough et al., 2009; Meier and Larner, 2014; Wegrzyn et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work on mitochondrial localization of STAT proteins.

claim: Upon activation, mitochondrial outer membrane PKAc begins to gradually diffuse throughout the cell.
source: Studies have demonstrated that, upon activation, mitochondrial OM PKAc begins to gradually diffuse throughout the cell (Webb et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work on PKAc diffusion.

claim: The non-stoichiometric increase in PKAc compared to PKAr expression is consistent with a dynamic signaling event.
source: Thus, the non-stoichiometric increase in PKAc compared to PKAr expression is consistent with a dynamic signaling event.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of differential PKA subunit expression and the known diffusion of PKAc.

claim: There have been no reported EPP-associated FECH mutations at the PKA target motif to date.
source: To date, there have been no reported EPP-associated FECH mutations at the PKA target motif.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of clinical knowledge.

claim: The low prevalence of EPP has made discerning genotype-phenotype correlations difficult.
source: However, the low prevalence of this disease has made discerning genotype-phenotype correlations difficult.
evidence: This is a statement about the challenges in studying rare diseases.

claim: PKA activity is implicated in the pathogenesis of a spectrum of hematologic diseases.
source: Our findings that PKA is an effector of EPO/JAK2 signaling implicate PKA activity not only in the pathogenesis of EPP but also a spectrum of hematologic diseases (Ishikawa et al., 2015).
evidence: This is inferred from the findings about PKA's role in EPO/JAK2 signaling and supported by a citation.

claim: PRKAR1A inactivating mutations are associated with metabolic syndromes in which anemia is prevalent.
source: PRKAR1A inactivating mutations are associated with metabolic syndromes in which anemia is prevalent (Stratakis and Cho-Chung, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work on PRKAR1A mutations.

claim: PRKAR1A deletion has the most widespread effect and is the only knockout of the PKA family with embryonic lethality in murine models.
source: This is in agreement with murine models where PRKAR1A deletion has the most widespread effect and is the only knockout of the PKA family with embryonic lethality (Stratakis and Cho-Chung, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work on PRKAR1A knockout mice.

claim: The mitochondrial expression of PRKAR2B is most dramatically increased in maturing erythroid cells compared to other PKA regulatory subunits.
source: Paradoxically, we found that it is the mitochondrial expression of PRKAR2B, and not PRKAR1A, that is most dramatically increased in maturing erythroid cells (Figure 1C–E).
evidence: This is supported by proteomics and immunoblotting data shown in Figures 1C-E.

claim: The dual role of PKAr is highlighted by the incomplete rescue of PRKAR1A-/--associated embryonic defects with PRKACA ablation.
source: The dual role of PKAr is highlighted by the incomplete rescue of PRKAR1A-/--associated embryonic defects with PRKACA ablation (Amieux and McKnight, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work on PKA knockout mice.

claim: PRKAR2B mRNA is selectively high in CD71+ early erythroid cells.
source: Indeed, there is both genetic and biochemical evidence supporting a pivotal and specific role for PRKAR2B in blood development and disease. Global transcriptome analysis has shown that PRKAR2B mRNA is selectively high in CD71+ early erythroid cells (Su et al., 2004) and PRKAR2B binds with higher affinity than PRKAR1A to AKAP10 (Burns et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous transcriptome analysis.

claim: PRKAR2B binds with higher affinity than PRKAR1A to AKAP10.
source: Indeed, there is both genetic and biochemical evidence supporting a pivotal and specific role for PRKAR2B in blood development and disease. Global transcriptome analysis has shown that PRKAR2B mRNA is selectively high in CD71+ early erythroid cells (Su et al., 2004) and PRKAR2B binds with higher affinity than PRKAR1A to AKAP10 (Burns et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous biochemical work.

claim: AKAP10 polymorphisms correlate with human blood traits in genome-wide association studies.
source: The latter point is particularly important given the recent correlation of AKAP10 polymorphisms with human blood traits in genome-wide association studies (Gieger et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a genome-wide association study.

claim: AKAP10 encodes many isoforms that may localize to different subcellular compartments.
source: It is also notable that AKAP10 encodes many isoforms that may localize to different subcellular compartments (Eggers et al., 2009; Huang et al., 1997a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work on AKAP10 isoforms.

claim: Non-mitochondrial AKAP10 isoforms may function in a variety of contexts both in hematopoiesis and in other aspects of development including the cardiovascular system.
source: Although our CRISPR targeting strategy was designed to specifically disrupt the N-terminal mitochondrial-targeting motif (Figure 2G), non-mitochondrial AKAP10 isoforms may function in a variety of contexts both in hematopoiesis and in other aspects of development including the cardiovascular system (Kammerer et al., 2003; Tingley et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a speculation supported by citations to previous work on AKAP10 function.

claim: Perturbations in PKA signaling have significant impact on human health including the pathogenesis of hematologic diseases.
source: Our work, here, provides further evidence that perturbations in PKA signaling have significant impact on human health (Kammerer et al., 2003) including the pathogenesis of hematologic diseases that, to date, has been unappreciated and warrants further investigation.
evidence: This is inferred from the findings of the study and supported by a citation.
